extracted.intended_audience: students of logic, philosophers, and readers learning formal reasoning
extracted.subtask_description: Guidelines and criteria for constructing, analysing, and assessing reasoning (syllogistic ratiocination and induction), including formal requirements for syllogisms, distinctions between kinds of inference, and the underlying axioms that ground logical legitimacy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinction between Induction and Ratiocination (Syllogism)
rubrics_metrics.description: Reasoning is popularly of two kinds: reasoning from particulars to generals (Induction) and reasoning from generals to particulars (Ratiocination or Syllogism); a third species exists which underlies both.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Induction: inferring a proposition from propositions less general than itself (ascending from individual instances to a general law). Ratiocination: inferring a proposition from propositions equally or more general (combining general propositions to infer another of same or lesser generality, or a particular). The conclusion is called Induction when it is more general than the largest premise, and Ratiocination when it is equally or less general.

rubrics_metrics.name: Induction is genuine inference
rubrics_metrics.description: In every induction we proceed from known truths to truths which were not known; the induction's conclusion embraces more than is contained in the premises.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A principle ascertained by experience generalizes beyond the individual experiments forming its basis; it expresses belief that observed truth holds in an indefinite number of unexamined cases (including future facts). Conditions necessary for legitimate induction are discussed elsewhere; but induction is explicitly affirmed as a real process of inference.

rubrics_metrics.name: Three propositions requirement for a legitimate syllogism
rubrics_metrics.description: A legitimate syllogism must contain three, and no more than three, propositions: the conclusion and two premises which together prove it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is a formal requirement: syllogistic demonstration is structured as conclusion plus two premises; arguments lacking this structure are not proper syllogisms for the purposes described.

rubrics_metrics.name: Three terms requirement (subject, predicate, middle term)
rubrics_metrics.description: A syllogism must have three, and no more than three, terms: the subject and predicate of the conclusion and a middle term found in both premises which connects them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Major term = predicate of conclusion; minor term = subject of conclusion. Each of major and minor appears in exactly one premise along with the middle term. Violation of the three-term rule undermines proper syllogistic form.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of major and minor premises/terms
rubrics_metrics.description: The premise containing the middle term and the major term is the major premise; the one containing the middle term and the minor term is the minor premise.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Identifying which premise is major or minor is necessary for locating the major and minor terms and for classifying the syllogism's figure and mood.

rubrics_metrics.name: Figures of the syllogism (position of the middle term)
rubrics_metrics.description: Syllogisms are divided into figures according to the position of the middle term: first figure (middle term subject of major, predicate of minor), second figure (predicate in both premises), third figure (subject in both), fourth figure (subject of minor and predicate of major).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Some logicians use three figures merging the fourth into the first; classification affects naturalness and apparent conclusiveness of expression but not logical equivalence, since reduction rules exist.

rubrics_metrics.name: Moods of syllogisms (quantity and quality)
rubrics_metrics.description: Each figure is divided into moods according to the quantity (universal/particular) and quality (affirmative/negative) of propositions; only certain combinations (moods) are legitimate where the conclusion follows from premises.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The text lists all legitimate moods for the four figures with explicit exemplar forms (e.g., first figure: All B is C; All A is B; therefore All A is C; etc.). These enumerated valid forms serve as the canonical acceptable moods.

rubrics_metrics.name: Treatment of singular propositions in syllogisms
rubrics_metrics.description: Singular propositions are ranked with universal propositions for syllogistic purposes because their predicate is affirmed or denied of the whole of the subject.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: 'Socrates is a man' is treated like 'All Socrates are men' for constructing syllogisms; this explains why arguments involving singulars map onto the general moods.

rubrics_metrics.name: Validity criterion: truth of premises guarantees truth of conclusion
rubrics_metrics.description: A syllogism is legitimate in that if the premises are true, the conclusion must inevitably be so; the listed moods are precisely those in which this guarantee holds.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is the central test for legitimate ratiocination; the reader is referred to standard logic texts (e.g., Whately) for proofs of why only the listed moods are valid.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reduction to first figure via conversion
rubrics_metrics.description: All correct ratiocination admits of being stated in syllogisms of the first figure alone by applying rules of conversion (simple conversion or conversion per accidens) to premises.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: universal negative admits simple conversion (No C is B -> No B is C); universal affirmative may be converted per accidens (All B is A -> Some A is B). Reduction shows equivalence of figures and provides a normalization method for evaluating arguments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Two universal first-figure templates as universal types
rubrics_metrics.description: Two elementary first-figure forms are the universal types for all correct ratiocination: one for affirmative conclusions and one for negative conclusions, each with a universal major and an affirmative minor.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Affirmative example template: All animals are mortal; All men (Some men/Socrates) are animals; therefore All men (Some men/Socrates) are mortal. Negative example template similarly provided. These templates constitute canonical forms to which valid reasoning can be compared.

rubrics_metrics.name: Major premise must be universal; minor premise affirmative
rubrics_metrics.description: In the general formulas discussed, the major premise is a universal proposition (affirmative or negative) and the other premise is always affirmative, asserting inclusion of the subject in the class named in the major.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This structural observation explains how the attribute affirmed or denied of the entire class is transferred to the object(s) alleged to be included in that class in the conclusion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Analysis of propositions as factual (not merely classificatory)
rubrics_metrics.description: A proposition conveying real information asserts a matter of fact dependent on laws of nature (that a given object has an attribute or that two attributes co-exist), not merely the meaning of words or classification.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Critique of purely verbal theories (e.g., Hobbes): for syllogistic ratiocination to be genuinely informative it must recognize propositional content as factual claims; otherwise syllogistic inference would be mere tautology.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fundamental axioms grounding syllogistic legitimacy
rubrics_metrics.description: Two principles underlie legitimate syllogisms: (1) affirmative principle — things that co-exist with the same thing co-exist with one another (transitivity of co-existence); (2) negative principle — if something co-exists with another thing which a third does not co-exist with, the first does not co-exist with the third.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These axioms relate to facts rather than conventions and are the factual grounds of every argument where propositions assert matters of fact; they replace the narrower 'dictum de omni' as the true basis of syllogistic inference.

rubrics_metrics.name: Syllogism as practical 'mark' reasoning (attribute-as-mark formulation)
rubrics_metrics.description: Every syllogism can be reformulated: 'Attribute A is a mark of attribute B; the object has mark A; therefore the object has attribute B.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This phraseology (attributes as marks) is recommended as precise and powerful for expressing what ratiocination actually accomplishes in ascertaining truths. It also yields a unified form of the axioms: whatever is a mark of any mark, is a mark of that which this last is a mark of.

rubrics_metrics.name: Functional role and limits of the syllogism (petitio principii observation)
rubrics_metrics.description: There is a petitio principii in every syllogism: a syllogism cannot logically prove anything that was not already involved (however implicitly) in the premises; yet syllogisms often bring a person to perceive implications not previously acknowledged.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize both facts: (a) deductive limitation — syllogistic conclusion is implicit in premises; (b) epistemic function — syllogism publicly unfolds and makes explicit implications of accepted premises, thus serving as a method of conveying and clarifying knowledge. This tension informs judgments about the syllogism's epistemic value.

rubrics_metrics.name: Methodological recommendation on order of treatment
rubrics_metrics.description: When tracing acquired knowledge to its sources it is advantageous to commence with ratiocination (deduction) rather than induction (the earlier stages of constructing knowledge).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Starting with derivative truths and tracing them backward to their evidential premises clarifies dependence relations and facilitates examining foundations before discussing inductive origins. This ordering is recommended for the science aiming to trace knowledge to its sources.
